items.summary:
GuardAuthenticatorHandler::authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() logs a user in programmatically with a Guard authenticator, for example in the registration controllers that MakerBundle generated. This method creates the token and stores it, but it calls neither checkPreAuth() nor checkPostAuth() on the user checker of the firewall. Guard authenticators run both checks when they authenticate a request.

As a consequence, an account that a user checker rejects in checkPostAuth() could still be logged in through this method, for example an expired account.

Applications are affected when they use Guard with a custom user checker that rejects users in checkPostAuth(), and log users in with authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess(). The default user checker also rejects users of the deprecated User class whose credentials expired. This is the issue of GHSA-8f57-m8wj-x65w, for the Guard component of Symfony 5.4. Guard was removed in Symfony 6.0.

GuardAuthenticatorHandler::authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() now calls the checkPostAuth() method of the user checker of the firewall before it stores the token. AuthenticatorManager::authenticateUser() does the same since the fix for GHSA-8f57-m8wj-x65w. Like authenticateUser(), authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() doesn't call checkPreAuth(). Programmatic logins skip this check on purpose, for example right after a registration. SecurityBundle now gives the user checkers of the firewalls to the handler, so both symfony/security-guard and symfony/security-bundle must be updated.

As a consequence, an exception thrown by checkPostAuth() now comes out of authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess(). Code that logs users in programmatically may need to catch it.

items.summary:
The router redirects a request to the same URL with or without its trailing slash, or with the scheme that a route requires. To do so, the matcher returns RedirectController::urlRedirectAction() with the path info of the request as path. Since Symfony 5.4.44, 6.4.12 and 7.1.5, urlRedirectAction() turns a path that starts with // into <scheme>://..., so that protocol-relative targets configured in routes work. The path info of a request starts with // when its URI does. So these redirects send the browser to the host written at the start of the path:

GET https://app.example//evil.example/edit/  =>  301 Location: https://evil.example/edit

This affects routes whose path starts with a placeholder that accepts /, like /{path}/edit with the .+ requirement. The trailing-slash redirect applies to all of them, and the scheme redirect to the ones that require a scheme. A front controller in a subdirectory doesn't prevent it.

The matcher now encodes the slash or backslash that follows the leading slash of the path it redirects to, as %2F or %5C. It also does so when tabs or newlines come in between. The target route still matches it, and protocol-relative targets configured in routes keep working.

The matchers of the Routing component encode it too before calling RedirectableUrlMatcherInterface::redirect(), so that other implementations of this method get the encoded path as well.

items.summary:
The fix for CVE-2026-123339 (GHSA-wg5q-m2ww-f3c9) restores the router context of the main request after an inline fragment, but the cause of that issue is still there. A page can render an inline fragment with render() in Twig, or with an ESI tag when no gateway cache is used. While the fragment runs, SubRequestHandler adds 127.0.0.1 to the trusted proxies of every request. Code that reads the main request during that time trusts its X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded headers if the main request came from 127.0.0.1.

Symfony itself reads the main request there:
- asset() takes the base path and the scheme of the main request. With X-Forwarded-Prefix: //evil.example, asset('build/app.js') returns //evil.example/build/app.js, a script loaded from another host. Request::getBasePath() keeps its first result, so when it's first computed inside the fragment, the later asset() calls of the page return such URLs too.
- absolute_url() in Twig, through UrlHelper, takes the host and the scheme of the main request from X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto.

When a shared cache stores the page, every visitor gets these URLs. With asset(), the page then runs scripts from a host chosen by the attacker.

This affects applications reached over HTTP from 127.0.0.1 when that address isn't a trusted proxy. That's the case behind a TLS terminator, a reverse proxy or an HTTP cache running on the same host. When framework.trusted_proxies is not configured, which is the default, every forwarded header is trusted during that window, X-Forwarded-Prefix included. Configuring framework.trusted_hosts doesn't help with asset(), since the prefix is not a host. Applications that get requests directly through php-fpm or mod_php are not affected, and neither are those behind a proxy on another host. REMOTE_ADDR is not 127.0.0.1 there.

SubRequestHandler doesn't change the trusted proxies of every request anymore. Only the requests it builds, and the requests copied from them, trust 127.0.0.1. While a fragment renders, the main request keeps ignoring the forwarded headers sent by the client.

symfony/http-kernel now requires the version of symfony/http-foundation that contains this fix.

items.summary: Merchant underwriting becomes vulnerable when evidence is evaluated without enough visibility into its source, freshness, relationship to the applicant, or meaning for the proposed activity. Individually favorable checks do not necessarily establish that the same business is operating the merchant account, that its representative may bind it, or that its settlement instructions are authorized. We describe three failure modes of fragmented underwriting: distance from the source, the gap between a decision and the evidence needed to justify it; the correlation gap, in which material relationships among the person, legal entity, owners or controllers, representative, business activity, and settlement destination are not evaluated when each signal is considered alone; and point-in-time controls, in which a historical verification is treated as present eligibility. We map these failure modes to identity-proofing, customer-due-diligence, sanctions, third-party-risk, card-network, and Nacha requirements, and propose a merchant-underwriting application of the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture built on provenance, correlation, and persistence. The application keeps a logically unified evidence record that identifies what was checked, the subject and relationship involved, the relevant times, the applicable policy, the decision, and any exceptions, and it keeps evidence validation, applicant verification, organizational authority, and the institution's risk judgment separate. items.summary: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

items.summary: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.
items.title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise

items.summary: As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds. In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.
items.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.
items.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery

items.summary: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.
items.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries

items.summary: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
items.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis

items.summary: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. Once trained, the model supports efficient sampling-based attacks. On open-source targets, it achieves attack success rates comparable to state-of-the-art optimization baselines, while reducing generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer, it remains highly effective against proprietary systems, including 99% ASR on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and reaches 45% ASR on the substantially harder GPT-4o, more than doubling the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget. We further offer an intuition for why generative sampling can preserve high attack success, when the learned suffix distribution is close to the distribution of optimization outputs. Overall, our results show that learning adversarial suffix distributions yields a scalable, and practically efficient foundation for continuous LLM vulnerability discovery.
items.title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment

items.summary: Identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex translate authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. Due to their central role in authentication and trust mediation, a single vulnerability in a broker compromises every downstream service behind it. In fact, recent incidents have demonstrated that even widely adopted platforms are not immune to such issues, highlighting the critical need for systematic analysis. To build such an analysis, this work first defines invariants for broker operation. These invariants are not completely covered by existing authentication specifications, primarily because brokers are unique in their duality, i.e., acting simultaneously as a relying party and an identity provider. The invariants capture the properties that identity brokers must uphold throughout their workflows, as all 60 previous CVEs we consider violate at least one invariant. Within these workflows, we further define high-level action categories. Equipped with this information, our automated tool PORTA leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate API invocation sequences corresponding to the high-level action categories, and oracle assertions aligned with the specified invariants. PORTA identifies 33 previously unreported security vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers. We study these novel vulnerabilities and trace them to eight recurring patterns. We responsibly disclosed all discovered vulnerabilities: 29 have been confirmed, 14 patched, and 19 assigned CVE numbers, with 10 CVEs rated as critical.
items.title: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers

An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

items.summary: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.

items.summary: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.
items.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action

items.summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
items.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence

items.summary: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon\geq 0.5$) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon=0.5$, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. Code and data: https://github.com/Jamli58/fresh-keys-stale-secrets

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.
items.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems

items.summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
items.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models

items.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.
items.title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging. In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.
items.title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents

items.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) enable offline weight analysis and are reused as backbones in vision-language models (VLMs), increasing the risk of bit-flip attacks that manipulate stored weight bits to induce malicious model behavior. An adversary could identify vulnerable bits on a public LLM and later flip the same locations in a deployed LLM or its backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip is particularly practical in this setting because it is easier to achieve under hardware fault attacks than multi-bit flips. However, existing selectors are mostly limited to multi-bit flips, without in-depth analysis of single-bit flips. In this paper, we adapt representative data-free and data-based bit selectors to identify candidate bits. We evaluate each bit independently on source LLMs and at the same logical coordinates in backbone-matched VLMs (without re-search), considering both performance degradation and prediction patterns across multiple inputs. Results show impact of single-bit flips varies across selectors on LLMs and their backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip can make the model tend to produce a repeated output string across different inputs. Our robustness analysis reveals vulnerabilities in terms of performance and prediction patterns.
items.title: Analyzing Single-Bit Flips on LLMs and Their Backbone-Matched VLMs

items.summary: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
items.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code

items.summary: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.
items.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction

items.summary: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.
items.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents

items.summary: Third-party projects repackage free inference from LLM web applications and dedicated clients into independent APIs. We refer to such use beyond providers' permitted access, allocation, or redistribution conditions as LLM service freeloading (LSF). However, its scale and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We present a systematic measurement study of 513 open-source projects, tracing 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream LLM services and characterizing their development, dependencies, and operating mechanisms. We find that 93.0% of repositories were created in 2026. Direct HTTP or WebSocket requests account for 83.2% of paths, making reproduction of product protocols the dominant invocation method. Projects adapt messages, reconstruct conversation state, and convert responses to support compatible APIs. Account selection or rotation appears on 304 paths (19.1%), allowing projects with multiple eligible accounts to distribute requests across their separate allowances. Our policy analysis finds that 58 of the 62 services with available terms explicitly prohibit at least one examined practice, including automated access, account sharing, or service redistribution. These restrictions cover both downstream API provision and the means of obtaining upstream inference. Our findings inform defenses against unauthorized consumption and redistribution of free LLM resources. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to the relevant providers.
items.title: Demystifying Real-world LLM Service Freeloading

items.summary: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.
items.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings

items.summary: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). Four of the five victims leaked despite the policy. GLM 5.2 retrieved protected data in 64.3% of individual-attack runs and leaked in 0.6%: retrieval does not imply disclosure, but in high-stakes settings even one leaked field can identify a patient or client. At equal budgets, a larger red team is not automatically a stronger one; the victim model matters far more.

items.summary: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

items.summary: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports. We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. The agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe, with one run per commit, characterizing the direction and scale of the effect rather than its precise magnitude.

items.summary: Android kernels have long suffered from slow patch propagation from Linux upstream, with fixes often reaching devices far later than conventional Linux distributions. Until recently, this lag was largely a patch-management problem. With rapidly improving LLM agents, it is becoming an exploitation problem: public upstream patches can now serve as blueprints for building working n-day exploits before downstream devices are fixed. We test this threat end to end by building an automated pipeline that screens upstream Linux patches, reproduces memory-safety vulnerabilities on Android targets, and drives an LLM agent to construct local privilege escalation exploits from an untrusted application. Across 152 candidate CVEs reported over 33 months, we reproduce 38 vulnerabilities and generate 17 independently verified exploits under production defenses. Exploitation takes a median of 14.3 agent-hours and $321 in API cost, with 90% median reliability; 12 of 14 trials succeed on Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 devices. Notably, the pipeline relies only on publicly available, off-the-shelf models. Surprisingly, only 3 of the 17 exploited CVEs appear in Android Security Bulletins, suggesting limited visibility into which upstream fixes address vulnerabilities that affect Android kernels. For these 17 CVEs, the corresponding upstream patches reach Pixel devices with a median delay of 181 days. Together, these results reveal a stark asymmetry: attackers can increasingly automate exploitation in hours, while defenders still identify and deploy fixes on the timescale of months.
items.title: Aftershock: Yesterday's Linux Kernel Bugs, Tomorrow's Android Exploits

items.summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

items.summary: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.
items.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix use-after-free in oplock break notification

smb2_oplock_break_noti() reads opinfo->conn without any lock and
dereferences it after two allocations which may sleep.  When the
durable handle owning the oplock is disconnected, session_fd_check()
clears opinfo->conn and drops its conn reference under ci->m_lock, and
the last ksmbd_conn_put() frees the connection.  A break triggered by
another connection that races with the teardown can then resurrect the
freed connection: ksmbd_conn_get() is a plain atomic_inc, and the
queued break work later dereferences the stale conn via
ksmbd_conn_write(), a use-after-free reachable by any authenticated
client holding a durable batch oplock.

Thread the caller's inode into the notification path instead of taking
a new reference on it.  Every caller of oplock_break() already holds a
live ksmbd_file (or an explicit ksmbd_inode_lookup_lock() reference,
in the parent lease break paths) on the inode that owns the break
target's oplock list, so ci cannot be freed during the call, and its
lock can be taken without dereferencing opinfo->o_fp, which a
concurrent close may free.  Select and pin the connection under
ci->m_lock, the same lock session_fd_check() and
ksmbd_reopen_durable_fd() use to update opinfo->conn, so a concurrent
detach either loses the race to the clear or keeps the connection
alive until the notification work releases it.  Transfer the reference
to the work item and release it on allocation failures.

items.summary:
Description

`HostURLFilter.configure` reads the `ignoreOutsideDomain` parameter but tests the node belonging to
`ignoreOutsideHost` when deciding whether the domain mode was configured. A filter configuration that
names only `ignoreOutsideDomain`, which the class documentation presents as an independent mode, is
therefore discarded: the flag is forced to false, `filter` short-circuits on its guard and every URL is
returned unchanged. The filter enforces nothing while appearing to be configured, and the failure is
silent. The mirror-image configuration, naming only `ignoreOutsideHost`, fails with a
`NullPointerException` while the topology is starting.

The effect is the loss of a scope control the operator configured, so a crawled page's outlinks are
followed to hosts the operator intended to exclude. Impact beyond crawl scope depends on what the
crawler then fetches and is not claimed here. Projects generated from the StormCrawler Maven archetypes
are not affected, because all three shipped filter configurations set both parameters.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where each parameter is tested independently. Operators whose configuration sets only
`ignoreOutsideDomain` will find the crawl restricted to the source domain, as configured, which may
reduce the number of outlinks accepted.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should set both `ignoreOutsideHost` and `ignoreOutsideDomain`
explicitly in the `HostURLFilter` configuration, which produces the intended behaviour on affected
versions.

Credit

Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept.

Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated
and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

XML::Sig versions before 0.74 for Perl allow code execution via a document's Algorithm attribute that verify resolves to a function name and calls.

The text after the last `#` in the DigestMethod and SignatureMethod Algorithm attributes is looked up with Digest::SHA->can. That returns a code reference for any fully qualified function name, Perl builtins in the CORE namespace included. The digest function is called on the canonical form of the referenced element, so the document picks both the function and its argument.

An attacker who can submit a signed document can run a command as the verifying process.

items.summary:
TypesenseVectorStore is vulnerable to a document ID injection in its delete operation that can cause unintended documents to be deleted.



 TypesenseVectorStore.doDelete(List<String>) builds a Typesense filter_by expression by raw string concatenation of caller-supplied document IDs into the form id: [id1,id2,...] . The Typesense id field uses bare (unquoted) values in this list form with no escaping mechanism. An ID containing characters with syntactic meaning in the Typesense filter grammar — such as a comma ( , ), a closing bracket ( ] ), or operator tokens ( || , && ) — can break out of the list literal and alter the structure of the filter expression.



 An attacker who controls a document ID passed to the delete operation can use this to delete documents other than the intended ones (comma injection), or to construct a filter that matches every document in the collection (operator breakout), resulting in unintended bulk deletion.



 Applications that pass externally supplied or user-controlled document IDs to VectorStore.delete(List<String>) backed by TypesenseVectorStore are affected.

This vulnerability is due to the availability of memory write commands in the UEFI Shell while UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by selecting the UEFI Shell boot option at boot time and using available shell commands to modify UEFI memory variables. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, overwrite UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, and execute unauthorized software on the affected device.

items.recommended_action: 建议根据原文自行评估
items.summary:
The Grow R502-A fingerprint sensor driver (drivers/sensor/grow_r502a/grow_r502a.c) receives sensor responses in the UART interrupt handler uart_cb_handler(). Once the 9-byte header has arrived, the handler reads the 16-bit package length from the header and uses it as the byte count for further uart_fifo_read() calls into rx_buf.data. It never checks that length against the destination buffer. That buffer is a union r502a_packet on the calling thread's stack, set up by transceive_packet(), and is only CONFIG_R502A_DATA_PKT_SIZE + 12 bytes long (140 bytes by default).

A malicious or counterfeit sensor module, or an attacker who tampers with the UART wiring, can reply to any driver command with a header that declares a length of up to 65535 bytes. The ISR then writes that many attacker-supplied bytes past the end of the stack buffer. The existing length check in r502a_validate_rx_packet() runs only after the data has been written, so it does not prevent the overflow. Every sensor transaction is affected, including the ones issued by fps_init() during device initialization.

The result is a stack overwrite with attacker-controlled length and content in the calling thread. This can corrupt control data and may lead to arbitrary code execution on the host MCU, which would undermine any function the fingerprint sensor is meant to protect. items.summary:
The Grow R502-A fingerprint sensor driver (drivers/sensor/grow_r502a/grow_r502a.c) points drv_data->rx_buf.data at an rx_packet buffer on the caller's stack and enables the UART RX interrupt before waiting 1500 ms for a reply. When the wait timed out, transceive_packet() returned -ETIMEDOUT but left the RX interrupt enabled and rx_buf.data still pointing at the caller's buffer.

Once the caller's frame has returned, any bytes that arrive late on the UART are written by the interrupt handler uart_cb_handler() through the dangling pointer into stack memory that the thread has since reused. The bytes come from the device on the other end of the UART. An attacker with physical access who replaces or impersonates the fingerprint module can trigger this by delaying a reply past the timeout and then sending a packet. A slow or faulty genuine module can also trigger it by accident.

The result is a write of attacker-chosen bytes into a live thread stack. The write length comes from the header of the late packet. Commit 96968fac22b, which landed together with this fix, bounds it to a header plus CONFIG_R502A_DATA_PKT_SIZE bytes; affected releases do not have that bound. This can crash the device and may allow control-flow hijacking, depending on what occupies the reused stack region. The fix disables the RX interrupt, resets the RX semaphore and clears rx_buf.data on timeout, and the interrupt handler now refuses to write when no receive buffer is armed.

items.summary:
z_impl_pwm_capture_cycles() in drivers/pwm/pwm_capture.c stores its capture context (struct z_pwm_capture_cb_data, including a struct k_sem) on its own stack and registers a pointer to it as the driver capture callback's user_data. When called with a K_NO_WAIT timeout, k_sem_take() returns -EBUSY, which the function did not handle: it fell through, returned the uninitialized status field, copied uninitialized period/pulse values to the caller when that status happened to be zero, and returned without disabling the capture or clearing the callback.

pwm_capture_cycles() is a system call, and z_vrfy_pwm_capture_cycles() passes the caller's timeout through unchanged. With CONFIG_USERSPACE and CONFIG_PWM_CAPTURE enabled, an unprivileged user-mode thread that has been granted access to a capture-capable PWM device can pass K_NO_WAIT to trigger the defect. Without userspace the function is only reachable from trusted application code.

The uninitialized values come from the thread's privileged (kernel) stack, so a user-mode caller can read up to 8 bytes of stale kernel stack memory per call. More seriously, when the capture later completes, the driver ISR invokes z_pwm_capture_cycles_callback() with the dangling pointer. The callback writes into the expired kernel stack region and calls k_sem_give() on whatever memory now occupies it, which can corrupt live kernel stack frames and make the scheduler walk a forged wait queue. The result is kernel memory corruption from interrupt context, leading at least to a crash and possibly to privilege escalation out of the userspace sandbox. The fix rejects K_NO_WAIT with -EINVAL before any capture is configured.

XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 (ExAws.S3 module) allows an attacker to inject arbitrary XML configuration elements into S3 bucket-configuration request bodies via unescaped, caller-supplied values.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/s3.ex and program routines ExAws.S3.put_bucket_logging/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_notification/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_replication/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_website/2.

The bucket-configuration body builders construct their XML by interpolating caller-supplied values directly into the request body without escaping, and never route them through the module's own escape_xml_string/1 helper. A value containing XML metacharacters (<, >, &, quotes) can close the intended element early and open attacker-chosen elements, which the builder's trailing closing tag then closes, keeping the document single-rooted and well-formed. In a multi-tenant application where tenants configure their own bucket settings, an attacker who can influence one of the interpolated field values (for example the logging target, a notification ARN, a replication destination or Account, or a website redirect HostName) can inject arbitrary configuration nodes into a request the application signs and sends to AWS. The affected builders are reached through the public functions put_bucket_logging/2, put_bucket_notification/2, put_bucket_replication/2, and put_bucket_website/2.

This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.5.9 before 2.6.0.

items.summary:
XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows an attacker who controls tag keys or values to inject forged tag entries into S3 object and bucket tagging requests.

ExAws.S3.put_object_tagging/4 and ExAws.S3.put_bucket_tagging/2 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex build the <TagSet> request body by interpolating tag keys and values directly into <Key> and <Value> elements via to_string/1, without applying the module's existing escape_xml_string/1 helper (which delete_multiple_objects already uses for object keys). An application that forwards user-supplied data as a tag key or value lets an attacker close the intended element and inject attacker-chosen <Tag> entries. For example, a tag value of blue</Value></Tag><Tag><Key>owner</Key><Value>admin turns one intended tag into two tags on the wire. Because S3 honors tags in access-control conditions (aws:RequestTag, s3:ExistingObjectTag) and cost-allocation reporting, an injected tag can forge an authorization-relevant tag or corrupt the intended tag set.

This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.2 before 2.6.0.

items.summary:
When the proxy option isn't set, HttpClient takes the proxy from environment variables like http_proxy or HTTP_PROXY. On web servers, it ignores HTTP_PROXY, because PHP puts the Proxy request header there (the httpoxy issue). On the CLI SAPI, it read HTTP_PROXY from $_SERVER, where PHP also puts the environment.

This is the case of spiral/roadrunner-http, which the RoadRunner runner of php-runtime uses, and of baldinof/roadrunner-bundle and php-pm. A client could then send a Proxy header to choose the proxy of the requests that the application sent while handling its request. That proxy received the full requests to http:// URLs, with their credentials, and could forge the responses. For https:// URLs, it learned the host and port through CONNECT.

NativeHttpClient is affected since Symfony 4.3.0, AmpHttpClient since 5.1.0, and CurlHttpClient since 4.4.40, 5.4.7 and 6.0.7.

On the CLI SAPI, HTTP_PROXY is now read from the environment with $_ENV and getenv(), never from $_SERVER. Other SAPIs still ignore it.

The fix for CVE-2017-16652 restricts the redirects of HttpUtils::createRedirectResponse() to the host of the request. When framework.session.cookie_domain is set, it also allows the subdomains of that domain. To check a target, it read the host of the URL up to the first "/". But browsers also end the host at "\", "?" and "#". So with the cookie domain .example.com, a target like https://evil.test?.example.com passed the check, and the browser went to evil.test.

Applications are exposed when framework.session.cookie_domain is set. The default success and failure handlers of form_login redirect to the _target_path or _failure_path of the request. A login link can then send the user to another site right after a successful login, for example to ask for the password again.

HttpUtils now ends the host of a target where browsers do, before checking it against the allowed domains.

items.summary:
CsvEncoder::decode() splits each header cell on the key separator, . by default, and nests the decoded rows one level per separator, with no limit. PHP frees nested arrays recursively, so freeing data that is nested deeply enough overflows the C stack and crashes the process. With a stack of 8 MB, a CSV body of 448 KB is enough.

Each row also builds all the levels of its headers again. With a deep header, a CSV body of 2 KB made of short rows allocates more than 128 MB. A body of 1 MB keeps the CPU busy for 10 seconds or more.

Any code that decodes untrusted CSV with the Serializer is affected. From Symfony 7.4.0, this included every #[MapRequestPayload] argument that doesn't restrict acceptFormat, until 7.4.23 and 8.1.11 stopped decoding CSV payloads by default.

CSV headers can now be nested up to 512 levels, the default depth of json_decode(). Decoding also stops when the rows go through more than 16 header levels, or create more than 4 arrays, per byte of data. A header row of up to 5 levels always fits, whatever the rows contain. Beyond these limits, decode() throws a NotEncodableValueException, which #[MapRequestPayload] turns into a 400 response.

items.summary:
DoctrineTokenProvider keeps a copy of the previous token of a remember-me cookie. This way, concurrent requests sent with that token are still accepted for 60 seconds. The copy is stored in another row, under a series derived from the series of the cookie. Since Symfony 6.4.45, 7.4.18 and 8.1.6, a copy is stored for every series that the remember-me handler generates. Before, copies were stored only for the series created before Symfony 5.4.19, 6.0.19, 6.1.11 and 6.2.5.

A cookie could use the series of the copy instead of its own series. The copy then matched as a current token, so the limit of 60 seconds didn't apply and the theft detection didn't trigger. Logging out deleted only the row of the original series, and the copy stayed.

An attacker who got hold of a remember-me cookie could then keep logging in as its user after the user logged out. This works when the token was rotated at most once since the attacker got the cookie.

DoctrineTokenProvider now accepts only the series formats that the remember-me handler generates, whatever the collation of the database. It also deletes the copy together with its token.

items.summary:
Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted. It prevents a network attacker from stripping STARTTLS. But after the server's 220 reply to STARTTLS, the transport started the TLS handshake without checking whether more data had already arrived.

An attacker in the middle of the connection could add cleartext replies right after the 220. The transport then read them as if they came from the encrypted session. The attacker could make the transport skip AUTH, or report a message as sent while the server had rejected it.

Connections that use implicit TLS, with smtps:// or port 465, are not affected. Since Symfony 8.1, the Amazon SES SMTP transport enables require_tls by default on ports other than 465 and 2465. So ses+smtp:// DSNs are affected without setting the option.

The transport now refuses to start TLS when the server sends data right after its answer to STARTTLS, and throws a TransportException instead.

items.summary:
UrlGenerator puts the values of host placeholders into the generated URL without encoding them. Their default requirement, [^.]++, accepts /, @, #, ?, \, % and :. With the host {tenant}.example.com, the value evil%2Ecom# gives https://evil%2Ecom#.example.com/dashboard, which browsers send to evil.com. This works even when requirements are checked. Unicode full stops like 。 have the same effect, since IDNA maps them to ..

Applications are exposed when untrusted values reach host placeholders, for example when they pass the query string of the request to url(). A route that uses RedirectController::redirectAction() with keepQueryParams: true does the same, when the target route has a host placeholder that the redirecting route doesn't define.

UrlGenerator now rejects host placeholder values that contain a character that is forbidden in a host. These characters are C0 controls, space, #, %, /, :, <, >, ?, @, [, \, ], ^, | and DEL. Unicode full stops are rejected too. This check applies whatever strict_requirements is set to. When strict_requirements is false or null, the generator logs an error and returns an empty string instead of throwing. Host placeholder values can still be an IPv6 literal like [::1], but they can't contain a port anymore.

items.summary:
With the unanimous access decision strategy, an access_control rule that lists several roles requires all of them. That's the behavior restored by the fix for CVE-2020-5275. Since Symfony 5.4, the access decision manager asked each voter once about all the attributes of a rule. RoleVoter grants access as soon as the user has one of the roles. So a user who had only one of these roles was granted access:

security:
    access_decision_manager:
        strategy: unanimous
    access_control:
- { path: ^/admin, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_AUDITOR] }

Only attributes decided by the same voter were affected. For example, a role combined with allow_if still required both.

With the unanimous strategy, voters are asked about each attribute separately again, as before Symfony 5.4. Access is denied as soon as one of the attributes is denied.

CPU0                                      CPU1

dw_i3c_common_remove                 |
i3c_master_unregister(&master->base) |
device_unregister(&master->dev)      |
device_release                       |
//free master->base                  |
                                     | i3c_master_do_daa(&master->base)
                                     | //use master->base

Fix it by ensuring that the work is canceled before proceeding with
the cleanup in dw_i3c_common_remove.

items.summary: Federated learning (FL) assumes that a client can perform the computation required to produce its own contribution. This assumption is often unrealistic for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices, motivating designs that delegate some or all client-side training to more capable parties. We systematize this setting as delegated federated learning (Delegated FL), where data ownership and execution of owner-attributed learning are separated. We develop a framework that examines three dimensions over the same delegated transition: delegate-view privacy, delegated attribution, and constrained-owner feasibility. Our audit of 29 systems reveals a recurring composition gap. Privacy mechanisms protect selected artifacts without necessarily characterizing the accumulated view. Attribution mechanisms establish individual execution relations without necessarily binding the complete delegated transition. Furthermore, computational offloading does not establish whether the remaining workload fits the owner's resource budget. Two controlled studies on Raspberry Pi devices illustrate these gaps. We show that encrypted inputs can coexist with information leakage through an exposed residual and that locally retained labels remain inferable from split-learning gradients. We also show that message authentication can reject tampering without establishing that the executor performed the prescribed computation. Our findings demonstrate why individually established guarantees do not necessarily support the same end-to-end claim and motivate evaluating privacy, attribution, and residual owner cost over the same delegated transition.
items.title: SoK: When FL Clients Cannot Train -- Delegated Federated Learning for IoT

items.summary: The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.
items.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines
